column5: Concept
column6: Analogy

column3: Why do engineers write binary as hexadecimal?
column4: Long strings of 0s and 1s are impossible to read and easy to copy wrong
column5: Hexadecimal: every 4 bits become one symbol (0-9, A-F)
column6: A phone number split into short groups so you can read it at a glance
column12: Without hex, every address would be 32 ones and zeros and engineers would misread them; with hex it is 8 symbols. Scene: engineer at a desk misreading a wall of bits, then it regroups into hex.

column3: How does a computer subtract using only an adder?
column4: Building a separate subtractor costs extra hardware
column5: Two's complement: invert the bits, add 1, then add
column6: A car odometer rolled back one step from 0000 shows 9999, so going back is the same as going forward
column12: Without two's complement, every chip would need a separate subtract circuit: more silicon and more power in every phone. Scene: a phone plugged into a power plant (sight gag) shrinks to a normal charger.

column3: What is arithmetic overflow and how is it detected?
column4: Adding two big positive numbers in 8 bits gives a negative answer
column5: Overflow detection: the carry into the sign bit differs from the carry out (XOR of the last two carries)
column6: A trip counter that passes 99999 and flips back to 00000
column12: Without overflow detection, 100 + 100 could quietly become -56 in a bank balance or a game score. Scene: a bank app shows -56, the V lamp lights and catches it.

column1: Why your calculator thinks in decimal
column3: What is BCD and why do calculators and clocks use it?
column4: Displays and money need exact decimal digits; pure binary makes driving digits awkward
column5: Binary-coded decimal: each decimal digit gets its own 4-bit box
column6: Digital alarm clock: each digit has its own display, like each decimal digit getting its own 4-bit box
column12: Without BCD, every clock and calculator would need an extra converter circuit to turn binary into digits. Scene: a desk clock with a big gear-box converter that drops away.

column1: One extra bit catches a lie
column3: How does a parity bit detect errors?
column4: A single bit can flip in a cable or memory and nobody notices
column5: Parity bit: add one bit so the count of 1s is always even; an odd count means an error
column6: Washing machine that eats a sock: socks go in as pairs (even count, a spare added if needed); one lost sock makes the count odd, but you can't tell which, and two lost socks go unnoticed
column12: Without parity, one flipped bit on a wire would slip through unnoticed and corrupt a file. Scene: a photo sent across the desk loses a pixel; the parity lamp catches it.

column1: The counter that changes one bit at a time
column3: Why does a rotary encoder use Gray code?
column4: When several bits change at once, a sensor can read a wrong in-between value
column5: Gray code: neighbouring numbers differ in only one bit
column6: Turning a hi-fi amplifier's volume knob from 3 to 4: in binary all three bits flip (011 to 100), so the sensor briefly reads 111 and the volume blasts to 7; with Gray code only one bit flips (010 to 110) and the step is clean
column12: Without Gray code, a robot arm or a car's steering sensor could read a wrong angle for an instant and jerk. Scene: a robot arm jerks and knocks over a mug, then moves smoothly.

column1: Turn AND into OR with one trick
column3: What is De Morgan's theorem and why do designers use it?
column4: Chips are built mostly from NAND and NOR, so AND/OR logic must be rewritten
column5: De Morgan: NOT(A AND B) = NOT A OR NOT B, and NOT(A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B
column6: A two-door fridge light: it is on when NOT (left closed AND right closed), which is the same as left open OR right open
column12: Without De Morgan, chips could not be built from one repeated gate; they would be bigger, slower and costlier. Scene: a desk-sized chip of mixed gates becomes a small NAND-tiled chip.

column3: How does a Karnaugh map simplify logic?
column4: Every extra gate costs area, power and delay
column5: Karnaugh map: put the truth table on a grid and circle neighbouring 1s to merge terms
column6: A 2x4 egg carton is a 3-variable K-map: eggs are the 1s, and one band around neighbouring eggs replaces several gates with one term
column12: Without simplification, chips would carry extra gates: more area, more power, more delay. Scene: a hot, slow chip with a roaring fan becomes a small, cool chip.

column3: What are don't-care conditions?
column4: Some input codes never occur (BCD 10-15), yet a plain design still spends gates on them
column5: Don't-care: treat impossible inputs as 0 or 1, whichever makes the circuit smaller
column6: A traffic light: red and green never light together, so drivers only look at green and never check that red is off. Three lamps = 3 bits R Y G; go = G·R'·Y' (3 gates); the impossible patterns 011, 101, 111 are don't-cares (X), one loop round the 2x2 block gives Go = G: one wire, no gate

column3: What are noise margins?
column4: Wires pick up noise; an analog signal is corrupted by every bump
column5: Noise margins: a safe gap between the highest valid 0 and the lowest valid 1
column6: A road with a wide grass strip between two lanes: small swerves never cross into the other lane

column1: Car one shakes, but in car five, you don't.
column3: What is the regenerative property of logic gates?
column4: A noisy signal passed through 20 gates should get worse, but it does not
column5: Regeneration: each gate's steep transfer curve pushes a weak level back to a clean 0 or 1
column6: A convoy of five numbered supercars. First the copying world: a dog runs out, car 1 shakes, each car copies and adds, so car 5 crosses the line. Then real drivers: they copy the lane change but steer by the lane lines, so car 5 drives straight. Car = gate, lane = bit (1 high, 0 low), the middle line = the switching point where the gate is steep; inside a lane it is flat, and it builds its output from its own power wire

column1: You add two numbers, but each column adds three.
column3: How does a full adder work?
column4: Computers must add multi-bit numbers using only gates
column5: Full adder: sum = A XOR B XOR Cin, carry = majority of A, B, Cin; chain them for n bits
column6: Column addition on paper: every column adds three numbers (two digits plus the carry), writes the last digit and carries the rest. In bits a column's total is 0 to 3: sum = an odd number of ones (XOR), carry = at least two ones (majority); each column is one full adder, chained right to left (ripple carry). 58 + 67 = 125; 0110 + 0111 = 1101

column1: Three switches, eight doorbells, but you never ring two.
column3: What does a decoder do in a memory chip?
column4: Out of millions of locations, exactly one must be picked from a short address
column5: Decoder: n input bits select exactly one of 2^n outputs
column6: A small building's intercom: the guard's panel has three two-way switches (wing A or B, ground or first floor, left or right side), and every doorbell checks all three and rings only if all match its flat, so each setting rings exactly one of the eight. Switch = address wire (wing = bit 2, floor = bit 1, side = bit 0), flat = row of memory, "rings only if all match" = each row checks all the address bits, the ringing doorbell = the one word line that turns on, so that row is read; each extra switch doubles the flats (n wires → 2ⁿ rows, 20 → 1,048,576).

column1: Two sounds, one speaker, and your call never loses.
column3: What is a priority encoder?
column4: Several keys or interrupts can arrive at the same time
column5: Priority encoder: outputs the code of the highest-priority active input, plus a valid bit
column6: Your phone ranks its sounds (call above alarm above music above a message ping): a call stops the music even though the music started first, and hanging up brings the music back. Each sound is an input line (3 call, 2 alarm, 1 music, 0 ping); the speaker is the 2-bit output code of the highest line on right now; "is anything on?" is the valid bit (a silent phone gives 00 with valid 0, the ping alone 00 with valid 1).

column1: Two taps fight over your tank, but nobody wins.
column3: What is a tri-state buffer and why does a bus need it?
column4: Several devices share one bus; two driving at once short each other
column5: Three-state output: 0, 1 or high impedance (disconnected)
column6: One tank shared by three tap pairs (fill tap from a high supply tank, drain tap to the floor, a lock and a gauge each): if pair one fills while pair two drains, water rushes through and the level sticks in between, so all but one pair lock both taps shut and only read the level. Tank = bus, tap pair = a chip's output (fill = PMOS to VDD, drain = NMOS to ground), lock = enable; both taps locked = high impedance (Z), the third state.

column1: Handle at half, but your tank won't fill half.
column3: What sets the switching threshold of a CMOS inverter?
column4: PMOS carries current about 2-3x worse than NMOS, so the inverter flips off-centre
column5: Switching threshold VM: size the PMOS wider to centre VM at VDD/2
column6: One handle opens the top (fill) tap from a high tank as it shuts the bottom (drain) tap; halfway both run and the level settles where in = out, but the narrower fill pipe loses, so the tank sits low; widen the fill pipe and halfway means half full. Handle = input voltage, fill tap from the high tank = PMOS to VDD, drain tap = NMOS to ground, level = output, pipe width = transistor width W, handle position where the level sits at half = switching threshold VM (same size, 1 V say: about 0.45 V; PMOS about 2.5x wider: 0.50 V).

column1: Half the floors, you climb a quarter, not half.
column3: Why does lowering supply voltage save so much power?
column4: Phones and laptops burn battery every time a gate switches
column5: Dynamic power P = a·C·VDD²·f: energy goes with the square of the voltage
column6: Carrying buckets up the stairs to fill a tall tank from the roof: the tank is as tall as the building, one bucket per floor of tank, and every bucket is carried up to the roof. Half-height building: half the buckets (charge = C x V) and each climbs half the floors (voltage), so 2 x 2 = 4 floors climbed instead of 4 x 4 = 16. Tank = the wire's store, bucket = drop of charge, floors = voltage, climbing = energy from the supply.

column1: A slow turn costs you ten times the water.
column3: What is short-circuit power in CMOS?
column4: During a slow input edge, both transistors are on for a moment and current flows straight from VDD to GND
column5: Short-circuit current: keep input and output edges sharp and similar
column6: One handle swaps two taps (fill tap from a high tank, drain tap): a quick flick passes the middle in a blink, a slow turn leaves both taps half open so water runs straight through the tank into the drain, and a meter counts it (flick 1 cup, slow turn 10 cups). Handle = input, top tap = PMOS to VDD, bottom tap = NMOS to GND, glass tank = output, water through both taps = short-circuit current, cups = energy lost, turn speed = input edge (0.5 s vs 5 s edge: 0.2 s vs 2.0 s overlap, 1 vs 10 units).

column1: Your shut tap still drips. Why not zero drops?
column3: What is subthreshold leakage?
column4: A switched-off chip still drains the battery; lower threshold voltages make it worse
column5: Subthreshold current: grows exponentially as the threshold voltage drops
column6: A shut tap drips past its rubber washer; lift the washer one notch and half a turn opens the tap (quicker) but it drips 10x more (1, 10, 100 drops a minute). Tap = NMOS, washer = threshold, lifting the washer = lowering the threshold, handle turn needed = input that turns it on, drops = leakage current, drop counter = leak counter (carried through the fold); heat-jiggled electrons jumping a threshold step show why each notch down is 10x (lower jumps are 10x as common).
column8: 3.3.2 The MOS transistor under static conditions

column1: Your match never lights a log sixty-four times bigger
column3: How do you drive a large capacitive load quickly?
column4: A small gate driving a pad or clock net is very slow
column5: Inverter chain (tapered buffers): each stage about 4x bigger than the last
column6: Kindling a fire: a match never lights a log 64x bigger; you light twigs (4), twigs light sticks (16), sticks light the log (64), each 4x the flame before it. Match = tiny inverter, log = giant load capacitance, twigs and sticks = inverters 4 and 16, catch time = delay (load / width). One 64-wide inverter just moves the problem to its own 64 input. One inverter 64 vs chain 4 + 4 + 4 = 12
column8: 5.4.3 Propagation delay from a design perspective

column1: Double your ice tray. You never wait just twice.
column3: Why does wire delay grow with the square of length?
column4: Long on-chip wires are slower than the gates they connect
column5: Distributed RC line (Elmore delay): resistance and capacitance both grow with length, so delay ~ L²
column6: Ice-cube tray filled from one corner: each cup spills into the next through a notch. Tank = gate, notches = wire resistance, cups = wire capacitance. 8 cups: far cup fills in 27 ticks; 16 cups: 103 ticks (3.8x, heading to 4x for finer pieces). Fold: 8- and 16-piece RC wire, same 27 and 103 ticks.

column3: What are repeaters and why insert them in long wires?
column4: Global wires across a chip are too slow
column5: Repeaters: cut the wire into segments with buffers so delay grows linearly, not quadratically
column6: Pumping stations along a long pipeline keep the water moving

column1: When wires whisper to each other
column3: What is crosstalk?
column4: A switching wire disturbs its quiet neighbour and can flip its value
column5: Coupling capacitance between parallel wires; fix with spacing, shielding or not routing them side by side
column6: Two rowboats tied together: rock one and the other rocks too

column3: What is electromigration?
column4: Chip wires slowly break after years of high current
column5: Electromigration: electrons push metal atoms along, creating voids and hillocks; limit current density
column6: A fast river slowly carrying away its bank until it breaks through

column3: What is ground bounce?
column4: Many outputs switching together make the chip's ground jump and cause false switching
column5: L·di/dt noise in package and supply leads; fix with many supply pins, decoupling caps, slower edges
column6: Everyone in a building flushing at once makes the water pressure drop for all

column1: The short circuit a chip builds by itself
column3: What is latch-up in CMOS?
column4: A spike can switch on a hidden thyristor that shorts VDD to GND until power is cut
column5: Latch-up: parasitic PNP and NPN in positive feedback; fix with substrate and well contacts and guard rings
column6: Two doors that each hold the other open: once both swing, they stay stuck until you cut the power

column3: How does dynamic (precharge-evaluate) logic work?
column4: Static CMOS needs two transistors per input and is slow for wide gates
column5: Dynamic logic: precharge the output to 1, then let an NMOS network discharge it only if needed
column6: A bucket filled every cycle; you only open the drain when the answer is 0

column3: What is domino logic and why is it needed?
column4: Dynamic gates feeding each other can discharge by mistake
column5: Domino logic: a dynamic gate plus an inverter, so outputs only rise during evaluate
column6: Dominoes only fall one way and are set back up every round

column3: What is a Schmitt trigger?
column4: A slow or noisy input makes a gate chatter between 0 and 1
column5: Schmitt trigger: hysteresis, a higher switch-on and a lower switch-off level
column6: A thermostat that heats on at 19 °C and off at 21 °C, so it does not click every second

column3: What is switch bounce and how do you debounce it?
column4: A mechanical button bounces for milliseconds and the circuit sees many presses
column5: Debounce: an SR latch (or a timer) catches the first contact and ignores the bounces
column6: A dropped ball bounces several times before resting; you count only the first touch

column1: How a chip measures its own speed
column3: What is a ring oscillator?
column4: Foundries need a quick way to measure gate delay on every wafer
column5: Ring oscillator: an odd number of inverters in a loop oscillates with period 2·N·tp
column6: A circle of an odd number of people each flipping a card the opposite way: it never settles

column3: How does a shift register send data one bit at a time?
column4: Sending 32 bits side by side needs 32 wires
column5: Shift register: on each clock tick every bit moves one place; parallel-in, serial-out
column6: A bucket brigade: on every whistle each person passes the bucket to the next

column1: The counter with no decoder glitches
column3: What is a Johnson (twisted ring) counter?
column4: Decoding binary counter states for timing signals causes glitches
column5: Johnson counter: shift register with inverted feedback, 2n states, one bit changes per step
column6: A line of lights that switches on one by one and then off one by one

column1: Row and column not a million wires
column3: Why is memory addressed by row and column?
column4: A 1-million-word memory with one select line per word needs a million-output decoder
column5: Coincident (two-dimensional) decoding: one row decoder and one column decoder pick a cell
column6: Cinema tickets: row G, seat 14 finds one seat out of hundreds

column3: How does a Hamming code correct a flipped bit?
column4: Memory bits flip from noise or radiation; detection alone is not enough
column5: Hamming code: several parity bits over overlapping groups; the failing checks point to the bad bit
column6: Three overlapping circles of checks: the one spot where the failing circles meet is the culprit

column1: A chip you rewire after you buy it
column3: What is an FPGA?
column4: Making a custom chip costs months and millions
column5: FPGA: lookup tables and switchable routing configured by bits after manufacturing
column6: A LEGO base plate where you snap in new connections for every design

column1: The race inside a state machine
column3: What is a critical race in an asynchronous circuit?
column4: Two state bits change together; whichever is faster decides the next state
column5: Race-free state assignment: neighbouring states differ in one bit
column6: Two runners who must both cross a line; plan the route so only one ever has to move

column1: Why big chips cost so much more
column3: Why does chip cost rise faster than chip area?
column4: A bigger die fits fewer per wafer and is more likely to hold a defect
column5: Die yield: yield drops with area times defect density, so cost grows much faster than area
column6: Paint drops on a sheet of tiles: big tiles get hit far more often than small ones

column3: What is velocity saturation?
column4: Shrinking the transistor no longer speeds it up as much as expected
column5: Velocity saturation: carriers hit a top speed in high fields; current grows linearly, not quadratically, with gate voltage
column6: A short trip on a highway with a speed limit: a shorter road helps, but the cars cannot go faster

column3: Why did clock frequencies stop rising around 2005?
column4: Faster clocks made chips too hot to cool
column5: Power wall: voltage stopped scaling (leakage), so power density rose; the answer was multicore
column6: Shrinking a car engine with its fuel tank worked until the fuel stopped shrinking

column3: What is Amdahl's law?
column4: Making one part 10x faster barely speeds up the whole program
column5: Amdahl's law: overall speedup is limited by the fraction you cannot improve
column6: A road trip where only the highway gets faster; city traffic still takes the same time

column3: What is the principle of locality?
column4: Main memory is far too slow to feed the processor on every access
column5: Locality: programs reuse recent data (temporal) and nearby data (spatial)
column6: Keeping the books you are using on your desk instead of walking to the library each time

column1: The CPU that waits for memory
column3: What is the memory wall and how does a cache hierarchy help?
column4: Processor speed grew far faster than DRAM speed
column5: Memory hierarchy: small fast L1, larger L2/L3, then DRAM
column6: A chef with a cutting board, a fridge and a supermarket down the road

column3: What are the three C's of cache misses?
column4: Programs slow down from cache misses but the cause is not obvious
column5: Compulsory, capacity and conflict misses; associativity fixes conflict misses
column6: A small desk: first trip to fetch a book, desk too small, or two books fighting for the same spot

column3: What is the difference between write-through and write-back caches?
column4: Every write going to slow memory wastes bandwidth
column5: Write-back: update memory only when a dirty line is evicted; write-through: update both at once
column6: Editing a notebook and copying it to the master only when you hand it in, vs copying every word as you write

column1: Every program thinks it owns the memory
column3: What do virtual memory and the TLB do?
column4: Many programs must share one physical memory safely
column5: Virtual memory with page tables; the TLB caches recent translations
column6: Hotel reception maps 'your room 1' to a real room, and keeps a sticky note of recent lookups

column3: What is the difference between SRAM and DRAM?
column4: Caches need speed, main memory needs density
column5: SRAM: 6-transistor latch, fast, no refresh; DRAM: 1 transistor + 1 capacitor, dense, needs refresh
column6: A light switch that stays where you leave it vs a cup of water that slowly leaks

column3: Why does DRAM need refresh?
column4: DRAM capacitors leak and lose their bit within milliseconds
column5: Refresh: read and rewrite every row within a set window (for example 8 ms)
column6: A row of leaky cups topped up row by row before any runs dry

column3: What is a DRAM row buffer and why are row hits fast?
column4: Reading a DRAM cell drains it, and opening a row is slow
column5: Activate copies the whole row into sense amplifiers (row buffer); then columns read fast and the row is written back
column6: A librarian brings the whole shelf to your table: the next book from that shelf is instant

column3: Why does flash memory need wear leveling?
column4: Flash cells survive only a limited number of erase cycles and erase only in big blocks
column5: Block erase plus wear leveling: spread writes evenly across all blocks
column6: A whiteboard you can only wipe a whole panel at a time, so you rotate panels to wear them evenly

column3: What is Chipkill?
column4: In large servers, a whole DRAM chip can fail, not just one bit
column5: Chipkill: spread each word across many chips with ECC so a full chip loss is corrected
column6: Writing every word one letter per notebook across nine notebooks: lose one and every word is still readable

column1: Fetch it before you need it
column3: What is hardware prefetching?
column4: The processor stalls each time it reaches data not yet in the cache
column5: Prefetching: predict the next blocks and load them early
column6: A video buffering the next minute while you watch
column8: 2.2 Ten advanced optimizations of cache performance

column3: How does pipelining raise throughput?
column4: A long chain of logic limits the clock frequency
column5: Pipelining: registers split the logic into stages so a new input starts every cycle
column6: Laundry: wash the next load while the first one dries

column1: The CPU that guesses the future
column3: Why do processors predict branches?
column4: A pipeline stalls at every if-statement until the condition is known
column5: Branch prediction (tournament predictors) from past behaviour
column6: A waiter who brings your usual order before you ask
column8: 3.3 Reducing branch costs with advanced branch prediction

column3: How does out-of-order execution with register renaming work?
column4: One slow instruction blocks all the independent ones behind it
column5: Tomasulo's algorithm: reservation stations and register renaming remove false dependences
column6: A kitchen that cooks the quick dishes while the roast is still in the oven
column8: 3.4 Overcoming data hazards with dynamic scheduling

column3: What is multithreading (hyper-threading)?
column4: A core sits idle while it waits for memory
column5: Simultaneous multithreading: issue instructions from several threads to keep units busy
column6: A chef cooking two orders, switching whenever one is waiting on the oven

column3: Why are GPUs faster than CPUs for some work?
column4: Doing the same operation on millions of pixels one by one is slow
column5: SIMD / SIMT: one instruction controls many lanes in parallel
column6: One drill sergeant shouting one command to a whole squad at once

column3: What is cache coherence?
column4: Two cores keep copies of the same data and one updates it
column5: Snooping coherence protocol (MSI): a write invalidates other copies
column6: A shared class notice board: when one copy changes, everyone tears up their old copy

column3: What is false sharing?
column4: Two cores writing different variables still slow each other down
column5: False sharing: the variables sit in the same cache line, so the line ping-pongs; pad them apart
column6: Two people writing on different lines of the same page must keep passing the notebook back and forth

column3: How do systems stay up when parts fail?
column4: With thousands of parts, something fails every day
column5: Dependability: MTTF, availability and redundancy
column6: A plane with two engines keeps flying if one fails
